Description: Hor-Aha / Mene was the first king of Dynasty 1 and the founder of Memphis. According to Manetho, he reigned for 62 years before being killed by a hippopotamus. We have only fragmentary information about his successor, Djer's reign (Clayton 1994: 22). NB: following Alan Lloyd, no firm dates for the rulers of Dynasties 0 and 1 due to a lack of evidence. According to Ian Shaw, Dynasty 0 lasted from 3200 to 3000 BCE, and Dynasty 1 from 3000-2890 BCE.

Description: "In 1991-2 the tomb of the last king of the 1st Dynasty, Qa'a, was re-excavated at Abydos by the German Archaeological Institute, and seal impressions of Hetepsekhemwy, the first king of the 2nd Dynasty, were found in it. The German archaeologists have interpreted this find as evidence that Hetepsekhemwy completed the tomb of his predecessor and that there was no break in the dynastic succession" (Bard 2000: 78). However, Hetepsekhemwy means 'the peaceful one of the two powers', indicating that he may have come to power after a period of unrest (Williamson 2011). Description: Al-Mahdi was the first Fatimid Caliph. In 905 CE he was captured and imprisoned by the Aghlabids for proselytising Isma'ilism. After he was freed from his imprisonment by allies he fled from the middle east to preach his doctrine freely. Eventually he was able to supplant the Aghlabids as hegemons in Egypt, thus becoming imam and caliph of the new Fatimid Capliphate. He reigned until 934 CE, and was succeeded by his son Al-Qa'im.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Qa'im was named heir to the Fatimid throne in 912 CE and succeeded his father Al-Mahdi as Caliph in 934 CE. In 944 CE an Ibadi Berber named Abu Yazid launched a revolt against the Caliph that lasted until 947 CE. In 946 CE Al-Qa'im died of natural causes and was succeeded by his son Al-Mansur. Coded Military.revolt: Present Abu Yazid Berber revolt of 944-947CE. Coded Military.revolt: Present Abu Yazid revolt upon succession.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Mansur inherited the Fatimid Caliphate from his father in 946 CE in the midst of a Berber revolt. Being an exceptional leader Al-Mansur successfully put the revolt down and was lauded by both Isma'ili (pro-Fatimid) and Sunni (anti-Fatimid) as an exemplary ruler. Al-Mansur suffered throughout his life with serious illness, in 953 he died leaving his empire to his son Al-Muizz.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Muizz had inherited the Fatimid throne in 953 CE from his father Al-Mansur. An inventive and tolerant ruler he made positive connections with the Coptic Christians under his protection. Al-Muʻizz was succeeded by his brother Al-Aziz in 975 CE.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Wilson 2004: 122) Wilson, John Francis. 2004. Caesarea Philippi: Banias, the Lost City of Pan I.B.Tauris.

Description: Regarded as one of the greatest Fatamid Caliphs, Al-Aziz inherited the caliphate from his brother in 975 CE. Despite his reputation as having a human and tolerant disposition the Caliphate saw extraordinary expansion in his lifetime, absorbing much of the Levant. Before his death in 996 CE, Al-Aziz enacted numerous military reforms which caused antagonism within the army erupting into revolt upon the succession of his son Al-Hakim. Coded Military.revolt: Present revolt of the Maghāriba ('Westerners') and Mashāriqa ('Easterners') upon Al-Aziz’s death.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Cortese 2006: 120-121) Delia Cortese and Simonetta Calderini. 2006. Women And the Fatimids in the World of Islam. Edinburgh University Press. Edinburgh.

Description: “al-Hakin was murdered by his owner sister, Sitt al-Mulk, not only because of the threats his unpredictable behavior posed to the dynasty, but also because of his plan to make a cousin his successor, a move that would have violated the fundamental Isam’ili principle of father-to-son succession.”// It is likely that Sitt al-Mulk arranged for the assassination of the Caliph in collaboration with General Ibn Daws, whom she called upon after the Caliph had accused them of being lovers: 'In the course of this meeting she concluded a bargain with this military man and promised to share power with him in exchange for his doing away with the caliph.'; It is likely that Sitt al-Mulk arranged for the assassination of the Caliph in collaboration with General Ibn Daws, whom she called upon after the Caliph had accused them of being lovers: 'In the course of this meeting she concluded a bargain with this military man and promised to share power with him in exchange for his doing away with the caliph.' // With the help of Ibn Daws, she manage to have her nephew installed as Caliph despite the fact that he was a child and therefore not entitled to be a Caliph. After her nephew had been installed as Caliph, she called upon Ibn Daws in the presence of her viziers and had him killed accused of having murdered her brother. She then established herself as regent by appointing ministers loyal to her.

Description: After the suspicious disappearance of Al-Hakim, Sitt al-Mulk, mother of Al-Zahir, took over as regent running the affairs of state until her death in 1023 CE. Under Al-Zahir the Fatimid state plunged into crisis with famine and plague running rampant. Al-Zahir died from plague in 1036 CE, and was succeeded by his seven-year-old son, Al-Mustansir.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Daftary 2007: 193) Farhad Daftary. 2007. The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines. Cambridge University Press. Cambridge.

Description: Al-Mustansir was only seven when he inherited the Fatimid Caliphate from his father Al-Zahir in 1036 CE. During his reign state affairs were administered by his mother and her chosen officials. Between 1065 CE and 1072 CE Turkish invaders made inroads into Egypt subjugating Cairo and treating Al-Mustansir with contempt. Al-Mustali, Al-Mustansir’s youngest son became Caliph after his death through the machinations of the vizier Badr al-Jamali. Nizar ibn al-Mustansir launched a revolt shortly afterward. Coded External.invasion: Present Invasion of Egypt by Turkic mercenaries. Coded Intra.elite: Present Al-Mustali was made Caliph by the vizier Badr al-Jamali rather than the chosen successor Nizar ibn al-Mustansir. Coded Military.revolt: Present Nizar ibn al-Mustansir revolted
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Daftary 2007: 241-42) Farhad Daftary. 2007. The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines. Cambridge University Press. Cambridge.

Description: Al-Mustali inherited the caliphate in 1094 CE under the patronage of the vizier, Badr al-Jamali, and his son and successor al-Afdal Shahanshah. The usurped elder son Nizar ibn al-Mustansir launched a revolt in 1094 CE that was put down, but Nizar’s descendants continued to challenge the Fatimids for rule. Al-Mustali was subordinate as Caliph to the vizier Badr al-Jamali and al-Afdal Shahanshah. Al-Mustali died in 1102 CE, there were rumours that he had been poisoned, but little evidence of such. His son Al-Amir was proclaimed caliph shortly afterward.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Daftary 2007: 244) Farhad Daftary. 2007. The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines. Cambridge University Press. Cambridge.

Description: Al-Amir was proclaimed caliph in 1101 CE, at the age of five. The Caliphate was controlled by the vizier al-Afdal, who was assassinated in 1121 CE, Al-Amir took on an increasing number of functions which put him at odds with his viziers. In 1130 CE Al-Amir was assassinated and his son, Al-Tayyib, was sidelined in favour of his cousin Abd al-Majid, who after a complex coup and counter-coup, became Caliph under the name al-Hafiz li-Din Allah. Description: Al-Hafiz managed to wrest control of the Caliphate in 1132 CE. After a long a difficult reign Al-Hafiz managed to consolidate power, but the instability of the caliphate had been laid bare. In 1149 CE Al-Hafiz died from severe intestinal colic. He was succeeded by his only surviving son who took the name al-Zafir bi-Amr Allah.

Description: Al-Adid came to the throne as a child, after his father Al-Faiz died of a seizure in 1160 CE. His reign was dominated by the vizierate and he could only watch as the Fatimid Caliphate fell to pieces around him.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Daftary 2007: 250-51) Farhad Daftary. 2007. The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines. Cambridge University Press. Cambridge.

Description: Is this the ‘official story’? Was he poisoned and assassinated? ”Saladin formally put an end to Fatimid rule when ... September 1171, he had the khutba read in Cairo in the name of the reigning Abbasid caliph al-Mustadi ... thus proclaimng Abbasid suzerainty in Egypt. ... A few days after these events, the helpless al-Adid, the fourteenth and the last of the Fatimid caliphs, and the twenty-fourth imam of the Hafizi Isma'ilis, died following a brief illness.” Coded External.invasion: Present Saladin's invasion of the Caliphate.
References: (Daftary 2007: 252) Farhad Daftary. 2007. The Isma'ilis: Their History and Doctrines. Camcridge: Cambridge University Press. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Lane-Poole 1906: 144-151) Lane-Poole, Stanley. 1906. Saladin and the Fall of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Heroes of the Nations. London: G. P. Putnam's Sons.

Description: "Aybak then took another wife, daughter of the ruler of Mosul. In April 1257, Aybak was murdered; Sharjar al-Durr was blamed ... and murdered in revenge."
References: (Nicholson 2004: 125) Helen J. Nicholson. 2004. The Crusades. Greenwood Press. Westport. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: “Aybak's Mamluks, the Mu'iziyya, raised Aybak's young son Ali as sultan, but then the Mu'iziyya leader, Qutuz, took over control as the first of a long line of Mamluk sultans."
References: (Nicholson 2004: 125) Helen J. Nicholson. 2004. The Crusades. Greenwood Press. Westport. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Description: "Qutuz himself worried constantly about dissension ... Open hostility dogged his relations with the Salihiyyah and Ashrafiyyah as well as their constituents in the army of Egypt. ... Qutuz was assassinated, however, before his patronage of these non-khushdashiyyah clients could produce any dividends. On the whole, exile, arrest and confiscation seem to have been the hallmarks of Qutuz's relations with the Mamluk elite."
References: (Clifford 2013: 79-80) Winslow Williams Clifford. 2013. Edited by Stephan Conermann. State formation and the structure of politics in Mamluk Syro-Egypt, 648–741 A.H./1250 - 1340 C.E. Description: Al-Said Baraka Khan inherited the Mamluk Sultunate from his father Al-Zahir Baybars I in 1277 CE. The succession was uneventful, but Al-Said Baraka Khan was forced to abdicate in 1279 CE.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Asbridge 2010: 108) Asbridge, Thomas. 2010. The Crusades: The War for the Holy Land. Simon and Schuster. $ (Northrup 1998: 84) Northrup, Linda. 1998. Description: Al-Said Baraka Khan was deposed in 1279 CE, "The new mamluk sultan, Baraka Khan ... proved to be incapable of living up to his father's legacy, and his reign was cut short in 1279 by a group of senior officers led by Qalawun, Baybar's close associate.” In his place the seven-year-old Al-Adil Salamish was made Sultan.
References: (Mikaberidze 2011: 559) Alexander Mikaberidze. ed. 2011. Conflict and Conquest in the Islamic World: A Historical Encyclopedia, Volume 1. ABC-CLIO. Santa Barbara. $ John E Morby. 2018. Description: Al-Adil Salamish was deposed shortly after asending to Sultan, “al-Malik al-Adil Badr al-Din Solamish (1279-80) was seven years old when he ascended the throne. Kalawan was his regent who then deposed him in 1280.” Al-Mansur Qalaun took over as Sultan.
References: (Torsello 2011: 380) Marino Sanudo Torsello. 2011. Peter Lock trans. The Book of the Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross. Ashgate Publishing Limited. Farnham. $ John E Morby. 2018. Description: Al-Mansur Qalaun ruled from 1279 CE until 1290 CE. His heir was his eledest son Al-Ashraf Khalil, whom he distrusted. Sources disagree whether he died of illness or was poisoned, but the succesion was smooth.
References: p. 158 Linda S Northrup. 1998. From Slave to Sultan: The Career of Al-Manṣūr Qalāwūn and the Consolidation of Mamluk Rule in Egypt and Syria (678-689 A.H./1279-1290 A.D.). Franz Steiner Verlag. Stuttgart. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Sultan Khalil was "assassinated in 1293, aged twenty-nine, by three of his own officers." He was succeeded by his nine-year-old borther Al-Nasir Muhammad I.
References: Susan Wise Bauer. 2013. The History of the Renaissance World: From the Rediscovery of Aristotle to the Conquest of Constantinople. W. W. Norton & Company. New York. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Nicolle 2005: 26) Nicolle, D. 2005. Acre 1291: Bloody Sunset of the Crusader States. Osprey Publishing.

Description: Al-Adil Kitbugha usurped al-Nasir Muhammad in 1294 CE. Later in Kitbugha's reign he was deposed by Al-Mansur Lajin.
References: (Northrup 1998, 252) Northrup, Linda S. (1998). "The Bahri Mamluk sultanate". In Petry, Carl F. The Cambridge History of Egypt, Vol. 1: Islamic Egypt 640-1517. Cambridge University Press. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Al-Hijji 1976: 7) H. Al-Hijji. 1976. Description: Lajin had deposed his former lord Al-Adil Kitbugha and taken the throne for himself.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Northrup 1998: 252) Northrup, Linda S. 1998. "The Bahri Mamluk sultanate". In Petry, Carl F. The Cambridge History of Egypt, Vol. 1: Islamic Egypt 640-1517. Cambridge University Press.

Description: "In a bid to consolidate his control, Lajin attempted to redistribute iqtaʿat to his supporters. Lajin was unable to retain the sultanate”, “al-Nasir Muhammad was restored to power in 1298”.
References: (Northrup 1998: 252) Northrup, Linda S. 1998. "The Bahri Mamluk sultanate". In Petry, Carl F. The Cambridge History of Egypt, Vol. 1: Islamic Egypt 640-1517. Cambridge University Press. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: “Lajin was unable to retain the sultanate and al-Nasir Muhammad was restored to power in 1298, ruling a fractious realm until being toppled a second time by Baybars II, a Circassian mamluk of Qalawun, who was known to be more wealthy, pious and cultured than his immediate predecessors.”; Abdicated
References: (Northrup 1998, 252) Northrup, Linda S. (1998). "The Bahri Mamluk sultanate". In Petry, Carl F. The Cambridge History of Egypt, Vol. 1: Islamic Egypt 640-1517. Cambridge University Press. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Bonn University Press.

Description: "After al-Nasir Muhammad repeated to Baybars al-Jashnakir all the evils that the latter had done to him, Baybars al-Jashnakir was executed, probably by strangling ... April 1310."
References: (Mazor 2015: 197) Amir Mazor. 2015. The Rise and Fall of a Muslim Regiment: The Manṣūriyya in the First Mamluk Sultanate, 678/1279–741/1341. Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Abu Bakr inherited the Sultanate from his father Al-Nasir Muhammad I in 1341 CE. Although Sultan, most of the power in the realm rested with Al-Nasir’s senior emirs.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Joseph Drory. 2006. "The prince who favored the desert." David J Wasserstein. Ami Ayalon. eds. Mamluks and Ottomans: Studies in Honour of Michael Winter. Routledge. London.

Description: Abu Bakr made attempts at reforming the Mamluk Sultunate, but was quickly foiled by the powerful emirs. "... Abu Bakr, less than 20 years old, was meant to be merely a puppet. ... He was concerned lest he be imprisoned by a too self-reliant Abu Bakr. Perhaps just an excuse, in any case it prompted Qawsun to detail Abu Bakr ... on the invented pretext of frivolous behavior. Abu Bakr was sent, together with six of his brothers, to distant Qus, where he was executed...". He was succeeded by Al-Nasir Muhammad I's son, Al-Ashraf Kujkuk.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Joseph Drory. 2006. "The prince who favored the desert." David J Wasserstein. Ami Ayalon. eds. Mamluks and Ottomans: Studies in Honour of Michael Winter. Routledge. London.

Description: The nine year old Kujuk "declared Sultan already in early ... January 1341” and was murdered a year later in 1345 CE. In his place Al-Nasir Ahmad I became Sultan, but he lasted only a few months before being deposed and replaced by his brother Al-Salih Ismail.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Joseph Drory. 2006. "The prince who favored the desert." David J Wasserstein. Ami Ayalon. eds. Mamluks and Ottomans: Studies in Honour of Michael Winter. Routledge. London.

Description: Al-Salih Ismail inherited the Sultanate from his brother an-Nasir Ahmad in 1342 CE. He was taken ill in 1344 and died in 1345 CE, being succeeded by his brother Al-Kamil Shaban I.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ (Holt 1986: 123) Peter Malcolm Holt. 1986. The Age of the Crusades: The Near East from the Eleventh Century to 1517. Longman.

Description: Shortly after taking the throne, “A revolt broke out in Jumada II 747/ September 1346, and al-Kamil Sha'ban was captured and put to death”. His successor was Al-Muzaffar Hajji I.
References: p. 123 Peter Malcolm Holt. 1986. The Age of the Crusades: The Near East from the Eleventh Century to 1517. Longman. $ John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Muzaffar Hajji I inherited the Mamluk throne in 1346 CE after his brother Al-Kamil Shaban I was killed. Hajji I was unpopular with the emirs, who thought he was neglecting his duties with gambling and sports. He was betrayed by his troops and killed by agents of the emirs that he had planned to deposed. He was succeeded by his brother Al-Nasir al-Hasan.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: In the first of Al-Nasir al-Hasan’s reigns he was a mere figurehead, with the Sultanate being controlled by the emirs. Al-Hasan made an attempt to supplant the emirs after the coming of the Black Death, but in 1351 CE, Taz, the principle strongman behind the throne ousted him as Sultan and replaced him with his brother Al-Salih Salih.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Howyda N. Al-Harithy. 1996. "The Complex of Sultan Hasan in Cairo: Reading Between the Lines". In Gibb, H.A.R. $ E. van Donzel $ P.J. Bearman $ J. van Lent (eds.). The Encyclopaedia of Islam. ISBN 9789004106338.

Description: Al-Salih was appointed as sultan in place of his half-brother an-Nasir Hasan after being deposed in 1351 CE. In effect the emirs ran the Sultanate with Al-Salih as a puppet. In 1354 CE a plot by some emirs saw the overthrow of Taz, the effective ruler of the Sultanate, and the deposition of Al-Salih. He was replaced by his predecessor Al-Hasan.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Hasan spent much of his second reign politicking and eliminating potential threats to his rule. In 1361 CE he was assassinated by military commander Yalbugha after regaining rule and trying to assert authority. He was succeeded by Al-Mansur Muhammad II, son of Sultan al-Muzaffar Hajji.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Levanoni, A., 1994. The Mamluk Conception of the Sultanate. International Journal of Middle East Studies, 26(3), pp.373-392.

Description: Al-Mansur Muhammad II was Sultan from 1361 CE until 1363 CE. He was deposed by the very military commander who placed him on the throne, Yalbugha. He chose his cousin, Al-Ashraf Shaban II to replace him.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Ashraf Shaban II was made Sultan in 1363 CE at the age of just ten. In truth he was a puppet to the powerful emirs, whom he ran afoul of later in his reign. In 1377 CE Al-Ashraf Sha'ban was killed in a revolt, the rebel Mamluk emirs installed his son al-Mansur Ali as Sultan.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Mansur Ali was another puppet of the powerful emirs, installed on the throne in 1377 CE. He died in 1381 CE and the regent and emir Barquq would have assumed the sultanate but the objections of the other emirs prevented it for now. In Ali’s place his nine-year-old younger brother as-Salih Hajji became Sultan.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: The young Al-Salih Hajji II was a mere roadblock for the ambitious Barquq, "During the subsequent reign of al-Manṣūr ʿAlī II (r. 778–83/1377–82), Barqūq was named atābak al-ʿasākir (commander-in-chief of the army) and used this position to gather allies and resources. When ʿAlī died, Barqūq placed ʿAlī’s eleven-year old brother, Ḥājjī, on the throne for a few months, as al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ (r. 783–4/1382), before deposing the boy and assuming the office himself."
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Schultz, Warren C., “Barqūq, al-Malik al-Ẓāhir”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, THREE, Edited by: Kate Fleet, Gudrun Krämer, Denis Matringe, John Nawas, Everett Rowson. Consulted online on 20 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_ei3_COM_24303

Description: In 1382 CE Barquq assumed the throne, overthrowing the young al-Hajji. Seven years later in 1389 CE a revolt by emirs saw Barquq flee into safety and al-Hajji was restored as Sultan.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Schultz, Warren C., “Barqūq, al-Malik al-Ẓāhir”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, THREE, Edited by: Kate Fleet, Gudrun Krämer, Denis Matringe, John Nawas, Everett Rowson. Consulted online on 20 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_ei3_COM_24303

Description: In 1390 CE Barquq returned from his exile and launched a revolt to once again depose al-Hajji. He was successful and ruled for another nine years, al-Hajji died in exile in 1412 CE.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Barquq died in 1399 CE after replacing many of his rivals and governors who opposed him. He was succeeded by his son Al-Nasir Faraj.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Wansbrough, J., “Farad̲j̲”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, Second Edition, Edited by: P. Bearman, Th. Bianquis, C.E. Bosworth, E. van Donzel, W.P. Heinrichs. Consulted online on 24 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_islam_SIM_2266>

Description: Al-Nasir Faraj had a tumultuous reign, as did his successors. He inherited the throne in 1399 CE from his father Barquq at the age of thirteen and was Sultan for six years before being usurped by his brother Izz ad-Din Abd al-Aziz. However Al-Aziz only reigned for two months before Al-Nasir Faraj was restored as Sultan. In 1412 CE Faraj was deposed once more by Al-Musta'in who became Sultan reluctantly. He himself was in the role only six-months before another contender, Al-Muayyad Shaykh, took the throne
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Petry, Carl Forbes, “Faraj, al-Malik al-Nāṣir”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, THREE, Edited by: Kate Fleet, Gudrun Krämer, Denis Matringe, John Nawas, Everett Rowson. Consulted online on 20 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_ei3_COM_26969>

Description: Al-Muayyad Shaykh took the throne in 1412 CE and died in 1421 CE. After his death there was a period of instability, with four different men occupying the Mamluk throne within one year. Immediately after his death Shaykh was succeeded by his son Al-Muzaffar Ahmad II, but he would reign for just seven months before being usurped by Al-Zahir Tatar. Tatar died after just a two month reign "from a chill contracted by paranoically wearing chainmail day and night...", he was succeeded by his son Al-Salih Muhammad III. He would reign from November until the following April, before being ousted by Al-Ashraf Barsbay in 1422 CE.
References: Irwin, Robert. “Factions in Medieval Egypt*.” Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 118, no. 2 (April 1986): 228–46. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0035869X00139917.

Description: Al-Ashraf Barsbay had a relatively long reign, ruling from 1422 CE until 1438 CE. His reign was relatively stable in comparison to some of his predecessors, despite the sultanate being struck by severe famine and plague. He died in 1438 CE and was succeeded by his fifteen year old son Al-Aziz Yusuf. However Yusuf would reign for only four months before being ousted by his regent and protector Al-Zahir Jaqmaq.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Zahir Jaqmaq was already sixty-five when he usurped Al-Aziz Jamal ad-Din Yusuf. He reigned until 1453, when he died at the age of eighty. He named his son Al-Mansur Uthman as heir, who ascended the throne in February 1453 CE. Uthman would only rule for two months before he was ousted by the emirs, whom he had alienated with bad behaviour and extortion. He was replaced with Al-Ashraf Inal.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Sobernheim, M., “Čaḳmaḳ”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, Second Edition, Edited by: P. Bearman, Th. Bianquis, C.E. Bosworth, E. van Donzel, W.P. Heinrichs. Consulted online on 21 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_islam_SIM_1584>

Description: At age seventy-three Al-Ashraf Inal usurped Al-Mansur Uthman and was proclaimed Sultan in 1453 CE. His reign was a particularly tumultuous one, with his Mamluk warriors making frequent raids on his own people. In 1460 CE a plague ripped through Egypt claiming Al-Ashraf Inal as one of its victims. He had named his son Al-Muayyad Ahmad III as his successor, but he would only rule for four months before peacefully abdicating after pressure from an alliance of Zahiris, Ashrafis, Nasiris and his own Mu'ayyadis. Ahmad was succeeded by Al-Zahir Khushqadam.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Zahir Khushqadam was Sultan of the Mamluks from 1461 CE until his death in 1467 CE. He came to power in a coup, deposing Al-Muayyad Ahmad III peacefully. Upon Khushqadam’s death Al-Zahir Bilbay became sultan, however he ruled for barely three months before being captured and deposed by Dhahiri Mamluks, who named Al-Zahir Timurbugha Sultan. Timurbugha, like his predecessor would only last a few months as Sultan before he himself was dethroned in a palace coup d’états in January 1468 CE. He was replaced with Al-Ashraf Qaitbay, who granted Timurbugha an honourable retirement. Immediately after Qaitbay's accession an insurrection boiled over in Eastern Analtolia, but was successfully put down in 1469 CE.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Levanoni, A., 1994. The Mamluk Conception of the Sultanate. International Journal of Middle East Studies, 26(3), pp.373-392. $ Holt, P.M., “K̲h̲us̲h̲ḳadam”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, Second Edition, Edited by: P. Bearman, Th. Bianquis, C.E. Bosworth, E. van Donzel, W.P. Heinrichs. Consulted online on 24 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_islam_SIM_4349>

Description: Al-Ashraf Qaitbay was Sultan of the Mamluks from his usurpation of Timuburgha in 1468 CE, until his death in 1496 CE. He was succeeded by his son Al-Nasir Muhammad IV.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Description: Al-Nasir Muhammad IV came to the Mamluk throne in 1496 CE following the death of his father. Al-Nasir’s reign was cut short, barely two years, before being deposed by Al-Zahir Qansuh I. Qansuh had been purchased by Sultan Qaitbay and made protector of his heir Al-Nasir Muhammad IV, which turned out to be a terrible miscalculation. In 1498 CE, after Al-Nasir Muhammad IV took over as Sultan, the Mamluks rebelled and killed him, electing Al-Zahir Qansuh I in his place.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Irwin, R., 1986. Factions in Medieval Egypt. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 118(2), pp.228-246.

Description: Al-Zahir Qansuh I would last no longer than his predecessor, reigning from 1498 CE until 1500 CE. Qansuh would meet a grisly end, being strangled on the orders of future Sultan Al-Adil Tumanbay. However, he was immediately succeeded by Al-Ashraf Janbalat who reigned from June 1500 CE until January 1501 CE; Janbalat was replaced by Qansuh I killer Al-Adil Tumanbay. Soon after his accession a revolt too place to remove him and his cruel methods. His replacement was Al-Ashraf Qansuh II an adherent and loyalist to the first Qansuh. Qansuh II immediately set about removing all of Tumanbay’s associates from the halls of power and soon found the deposed Sultan hiding with friends. Qansuh II had him executed putting an end to his revolt.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford.

Conflict.name: Battle of Marj Dabiq, Ottoman-Mamluk war
Description: Al-Ashraf Qansuh II saw the effective end of the Mamluk Sultanate, reigning from 1501 CE until his death in the Ottoman- Mamluk war. "The flight of the Mamlūk left wing, commanded by K̲h̲āʾir Bey (who was probably in secret understanding with the Ottomans), led to the break-up of the whole Mamlūk position. In the confusion, al-G̲h̲awrī fell from his horse and died, apparently of apoplexy. His body was never recovered." His death marked the end of Mamluk control of the middle-east and the rise of Ottoman hegemony in the region. He was succeeded in 1516 CE by Al-Ashraf Tumanbay II, who carried on the war, but failed to fend off the Ottoman threat.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Holt, P.M., “Ḳānṣawh al-G̲h̲awrī”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, Second Edition, Edited by: P. Bearman, Th. Bianquis, C.E. Bosworth, E. van Donzel, W.P. Heinrichs. Consulted online on 23 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_islam_SIM_3873>

Conflict.name: Ottoman-Mamluk war
Description: Al-Ashraf Tumanbay II was the last Sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate, reigning for only a few months before the Ottomans were finally able to subdue their long time enemy in the middle-east. He was executed in 1517 CE, and with his death the Mamluk Dynasty would come to an end. Egypt was incorporated into the Ottoman Empire and administrated by a Pasha. The Sultanate would eventually be revived in the 19th Century under a different dynasty.
References: John E Morby. 2018. Dynasties of the World. A Chronological and Genealogical Handbook. Oxford University Press. Oxford. $ Holt, P.M., “Ṭūmān Bāy”, in: Encyclopaedia of Islam, Second Edition, Edited by: P. Bearman, Th. Bianquis, C.E. Bosworth, E. van Donzel, W.P. Heinrichs. Consulted online on 23 February 2020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1573-3912_islam_SIM_7623>

Description: Amenemhat seems to have risen from humble beginnings to become Mentuhotep IV's vizier before overthrowing Mentuhotep to found the Twelfth Dynasty (Clayton 1994, 77; Callender 2000, 146). He faced opposition from 'recalcitrant nomarchs, Asiatics and Nubians on the southern frontiers', whom he 'crushed' (Clayton 1994, 79). He was murdered, possibly by his bodyguards (Callender 2000, 148). Amenemhat's son Senusret returned from the western desert and established himself on the throne (Clayton 1994, 79).

Description: Arguably the first known ruler of Upper Egypt was 'King Scorpion', who probably lived in the 31st century BCE and is known from finds at Hierakonpolis. He appears on a ceremonial macehead wearing only the crown of Upper Egypt, so he may predate the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Apart from this iconographic evidence, historians lack information on King Scorpion's reign, including how it ended. Narmer, who appears on the Narmer Palette and the Narmer Macehead excavated at Hierakonpolis, is the first known king of a unified Egypt. The palette portrays him as victorious over the common people, who are symbolized by lapwings. This suggests a rise to power through violent conquest, but we lack historical detail that would allow us to decide on many of these codes. NB: following Alan Lloyd, no firm dates for the rulers of Dynasties 0 and 1 due to a lack of evidence. According to Ian Shaw, Dynasty 0 lasted from 3200 to 3000 BCE, and Dynasty 1 from 3000-2890 BCE.

Description: Ahmose I, first king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, managed to reunite Lower and Upper Egypt, subduing both the Hyksos kings in the north and the Nubians to the south (Clayton 1994, 100-01; Bourriau 2000, 203). He also faced two uprisings within his territory, one led by a non-Egyptian (possibly a Nubian) called Aata and one by an Egyptian called Teti-an, who 'gathered the malcontents to himself' (Bourriau 2000, 203). Both intra-elite conflict and popular uprisings occurred as Ahmose seems to have faced opposition from both ordinary soldiers and those (elites?) faithful to the Hyksos kings. The power transition from Ahmose I to his son Amenhotep I seems to have been peaceful (Bryan 2000, 212-13).

Description: Thutmose I was not the son of his predecessor but a 'military man' who 'married into the royal blood line' (Clayton 1994, 101) and became king 'without event' (Bryan 2000, 220). The sources do not specify who may have led these. Description: Thutmose II succeeded his father Thutmose I and strengthened his claim to the throne by marrying Hatshepsut, his half-sister and another daughter of Thutmose I (Clayton 1994, 102). He had a brief reign and faced an uprising in Nubia by the local Kerma dynasts (Bryan 2000, 226-27). Hatshepsut wielded increasing power during his reign (Bryan 2000, 227), and when Thutmose II died, she began a co-regency with his young son by a harem woman called Isis, Thutmose III (Clayton 1994, 102-03). However, in later monuments commissioned by Hatshepsut, she claims that 'Thutmose I had proclaimed her [rather than Thutmose II] as heir before his death' (Bryan 2000, 229), so possibly she was already contesting Thutmose II's reign during his lifetime, or that may have been propaganda to secure her position.

Description: After Queen Hatshepsut died, Thutmose III once again 'came into his rightful inheritance', and some have even suggested that he may have been involved in her death (Clayton 1994, 107-08). Later on, he smashed many of his stepmother's monuments and the tombs of her courtiers (Clayton 1994, 108), suggesting that there may have been some remaining elite factions who supported the old queen. He also brought local princes in the Levant who had 'transferred their allegiance' from Egypt to the Mitanni Kingdom back under Egyptian control (Clayton 1994, 108). Whether his military expeditions also involved putting down popular uprisings in the Levant is unclear. When Thutmose III died, the throne passed to his son Amenhotep II.

Description: (No evidence for a transition period that was contested. Reign is 27 years. ‘Early’ could be after e.g. 5 years. No evidence overthrown.) Amenhotep II inherited the throne from his father Thutmose III (Clayton 1994, 111-12). Early in his reign, 'the Asiatic cities rose up in revolt', and Amenhotep was able to capture several rebel princes at Tikhsi (Clayton 1994, 112). Bryan (2000, 244) writes that his first Syrian campaign 'concentrated on the defeat of unaligned chiefs and rebellions among recently acquired vassals'. He also continued his father's work of obliterating the memory of Hatshepsut in order to 'eliminate' her family line's claims to the throne (Bryan 2000, 241). There is some doubt about whether his successor Thutmose IV was the legitimate heir; Amenhotep II did not take him into co-regency at the end of his reign, as had become a common practice (Clayton 1994, 113; Bryan 2000, 247)

Description: (Thutmose IV is considered a possible usurper but no evidence Amenhotep II was overthrown.) There is some doubt about whether Thutmose IV was the legitimate heir to Amenhotep II (Clayton 1994, 113; Bryan 2000, 247). Amenhotep did not take him into co-regency at the end of his reign, as had become a common practice (Bryan 2000, 247), so he may have been a usurper. Thutmose IV carried out minor military campaigns in Nubia and Syria (Clayton 1994, 114) and took 'punitive action' against the town of Gezer in Palestine (Bryan 2000, 250). Bryan (2000, 251) also mentions a 'desert police action' against Nubians who were blocking the transport of gold.

Description: Akhenaten inherited the throne from his father Amenhotep III and is famous for moving the capital to Akhetaten (el-Amarna) and venerating Aten, a previously 'minor aspect of the sun god Re-Harakhte', in its own right (Clayton 1994, 120-22). Van Dijk (2000, 269) writes that there 'must have been' opposition to Akhenaten's drastic reforms, especially among the priests of Thebes. He also 'sent his army to quash a rebellion in Nubia in Year 12' of his reign (Van Dijk 2000, 270). There is some disagreement about his successor Smenkhare, who may or may not have (briefly) ruled independently and could have been either his young brother or his wife Nefertiti assuming a masculine throne name (Clayton 1994, 126; Van Dijk 2000, 272).

Description: (Name change suggests attempt at conflict resolution during transition period i.e. ‘change his name or we overthrow him'.) When Smenkhare died, 'the very young Tutankhaten, the only remaining male member of the royal family, mounted the throne' (Van Dijk 2000, 272). Early on, his name was changed to Tutankhamun to signal a return to religious orthodoxy (from -aten, the sun disc, to -amun in reference to the sun god Amun-Ra) and the young king moved from Amarna to the old centre of Memphis (Clayton 1994, 128-29; Van Dijk 2000, 281). That he faced intra-elite conflict is suggested by the Restoration Stele, which describes the chaos that followed Akhenaten's reforms and hints that the army no longer supported these policies (Van Dijk 2000, 282). The army also dealt with rebellions/uprisings in Nubia and Syria during Tutankhamun's reign (Van Dijk 2000, 282). The king died young but it is still not clear how: a sliver of bone found inside his cranium have led some to suspect murder (Clayton 1994, 131). Either way, the accession of Ay, an old counsellor, to the throne seems to have represented an overturn of the agreed line of succession: Tutankhamun's regent and commander-in-chief Horemheb had apparently been given the right to succeed the young king if he died without an heir (Van Dijk 2000, 282-84).

Description: (If Ay died on the throne he wasn’t overthrown.) The accession of Ay, an old counsellor, to the throne seems to have represented an overturn of the agreed line of succession: Tutankhamun's regent and commander-in-chief Horemheb had apparently been given the right to succeed the young king if he died without an heir (Van Dijk 2000, 282-84). As such, Ay must have faced opposition from the army commander Horemheb and those loyal to him (Van Dijk 2000, 284). During his brief reign, Egypt faced Hittite incursions into its northern territories (Morenz and Popko 2010, 114), but the sources do not mention popular uprisings. Ay died after four years on the throne and his rival Horemheb declared himself king (Clayton 1994, 136; Van Dijk 2000, 284).

Description: Horemheb was of 'non-royal blood' (Van Dijk 2000, 285) but had served as Tutankhamun's regent and commander-in-chief, and had adopted titles suggesting the right to 'succeed Tutankhamun if he were to die without issue' (Van Dijk 2000, 282). However, Ay had instead managed to accede to the throne and had named an army commander, Nakhtmin, as his heir (Van Dijk 2000, 284). Horemheb evidently succeeded in the face of this opposition. He appointed another non-royal, his vizier Paramessu, as his heir, and when he died Paramessu succeeded him to become Rameses I (Van Dijk 2000, 285-86).

Description: King Horemheb appointed a non-royal, his vizier Paramessu, as his heir, and when he died Paramessu succeeded him to become Rameses I, founder of the Nineteenth Dynasty (Van Dijk 2000, 285-86). He had a short reign of only one year and the sources do not mention any contestation of his power or uprisings. He passed the throne to his son Sety I (Clayton 1994, 141).

Description: Sety I inherited the throne from his father Rameses I (Clayton 1994, 141). He led military campaigns in Nubia and the Levant and faced 'incursions by Libyan tribes' into the western Delta (Van Dijk 2000, 287). Vassals in the Near East switched their allegiance from the Hittites to the Egyptians, then back again (Van Dijk 2000, 287). When Sety died, the throne passed to his son Rameses II (Van Dijk 2000, 288).

Conflict.name: Succession to Merenptah
Description: Merneptah was the chosen heir of his father Rameses II (Clayton 1994, 155-57). He faced 'a "flash" revolt in southern Syria' as well as rebellions in Nubia and the 'western oases' (Clayton 1994, 157). When he died, his chosen heir Seti-Merneptah did not ascend to the throne; instead, struggles over the succession broke out and 'an unknown, Amenmesses, became king' (Clayton 1994, 158; Van Dijk 2000, 295).

The sources do not mention an assassination, but on Amenmessu's death the throne reverted to Seti II, probably 'the previously ousted Crown Prince', who erased the usurper's name from several monuments (Clayton 1994, 158).

Description: Saptah was the only son of Seti II (Van Dijk 2000, 296). Because he was young when his father died, he ruled in combination with his stepmother, Sety's chief queen Tausret, and a Syrian official called Bay (Van Dijk 2000, 296). However, Bay was executed in Year 5 of Saptah's reign, and Morenz and Popko (2010, 117) comment that '[i]n the succession of Merneptah we can observe two rival lineages competing for power'. Saptah died in Year 6 of his reign and Queen Tausret began to use the full pharaonic titles (Clayton 1994, 159). It was unusual for a woman to become pharaoh and the throne did not pass to a son of Saptah - this may suggest an overthrow.

Conflict.name: Disorder before accession of 20th Dynasty Egypt
Description: When her stepson Saptah died in Year 6 of his reign, Queen Tausret, who had been acting as regent, assumed the full pharaonic titles (Clayton 1994, 159). Tausret's effective co-ruler, the Syrian chancellor Bay, was executed in Year 5 of Saptah's reign, and Morenz and Popko (2010, 117) comment that '[i]n the succession of Merneptah we can observe two rival lineages competing for power'. After her death there may or may not have been a 'short period of anarchy' (Clayton 1994, 160; Van Dijk 2000, 296). Her eventual successor, Setnakhte, did not claim ancestry from Tausret, claiming instead to be chosen by the gods, and is considered the founder of the Twentieth Dynasty (Van Dijk 2000, 296-97). He described himself as putting down rebellions, but it is not clear whether these began before or after Tausret's death.

He managed to pass the throne to his son Rameses III (Clayton 1994, 161).

Conflict.name: Harem Conspiracy
Description: Rameses III faced incursions from Libyan and other tribes from the west as well as a large-scale invasion by the 'Sea Peoples' from across the Mediterranean and Near East (Clayton 1994, 160-61). His reign saw 'the first recorded organized strikes in history', by unpaid workmen at Deir el-Medina (Van Dijk 2000, 298). The Harem Conspiracy Papyrus also details a palace plot to kill Rameses III and incite a revolt outside the palace (Clayton 1994, 164-65). Previously it was thought that the king survived the coup or died during the judicial proceedings against the conspirators (Van Dijk 2000, 299; Clayton 1994, 165), but a recent examination of his mummy found that his throat had been cut (Hawass et al. 2012). Rameses III's successor Rameses IV was his son and crown prince (Clayton 1994, 165-66; Van Dijk 2000, 299).

Description: Rameses IV was the fifth son and crown prince of Rameses III (Van Dijk 2000, 299). During his reign, the influence of the high priests at Thebes grew (Van Dijk 2000, 300). There may have been trouble at Deir el-Medina due to late deliveries of 'basic commodities' (Van Dijk 2000, 300). Around 2000 soldiers accompanied a quarrying expedition, 'indicative of the amount of policing of the workforce required rather than any defence against attack' (Clayton 1994, 167). When Rameses IV died, the throne passed to either his son (Van Dijk 2000, 300) or brother (Clayton 1994, 167), Rameses V.

Description: When Rameses IV died, the throne passed to either his son (Van Dijk 2000, 300) or brother (Clayton 1994, 167), Rameses V. He faced a 'civil war' and workmen stopped digging his tomb (Clayton 1994, 167). During this time, the influence of the Theban priests was also growing and high priestly offices were becoming hereditary (Van Dijk 2000, 300), hinting at intra-elite conflict. Description: (No evidence presented that this king, based in Delta region of Egypt, was overthrown. 30-year-reign may suggest he died of natural causes and the state then broke up.) Rameses XI faced many problems: the High Priests of Amun at Thebes became virtually independent, famine struck, civil war broke out and the viceroy of Nubia (Panehsy) mounted a rebellion (Van Dijk 2000, 301-02). In Thebes, Herihor and his successor Piankh began to act as both High Priest of Amun and vizier, marking Upper Egypt's independence from Ramessid rule (Clayton 1994, 175-76). In the north, the accession of Smendes marked the start of the 21st Dynasty (Clayton 1994, 178).

Description: Huni was the last king of the Third Dynasty. He built his tomb at Meydum, 80 km south of Cairo, although it was likely finished by his successor Snefru (Clayton 1994, 40). In an apparently peaceful transition Snefru - possibly Huni's son by a 'minor wife' (Clayton 1994, 42), although this is disputed (Baud 2010, 66) - married Huni's daughter Hetep-heres, thus founding the Fourth Dynasty (Clayton 1994, 41-42). The sources do not give detailed information on Huni's accession and reign. Baud (2010, 66) writes that 'Although the line of demarcation between dynasties seems to have been permeable as far as blood lines were concerned, nevertheless the breaks between the 4th, 5th and 6th Dynasties could well have been linked to the accession of new families or branches of families to power'. NB: Lloyd's (2010) chronology section lists 'Neferkare' and 'Sanakht' between Khaba and Huni, but marks them with question marks.

Description: Snefru was the founder of the Fourth Dynasty, although he may have been the son of Huni, the last Third Dynasty king (Clayton 1994, 42; Baud 2010, 66). Description: Shepseskaf inherited the throne from his father Menkaure, perhaps because a more senior heir, Prince Khuenre, predeceased the old king (Clayton 1994, 58). Shepseskaf's reign was short and he completed his father's pyramid complex 'hastily' (Malek 2000, 91). The sources do not provide details on his accession or any contestations of his power. Description: Neferirkare inherited the throne from his father Sahure (Baud 2010, 66) and, like him, built his pyramid at Abusir (Malek 2000, 100). Baud (2010, 75) writes that the '"sun" kings of Abusir' had a more distanced relationship with the Egyptian elite than their predecessors, demonstrated by the separation of royal and elite burial sites. However, other than this, the sources do not give details on Neferirkare's accession and reign. The parentage of his successor Shepseskare is still unclear, but Baud (2010, 67) speculates that he was an 'older member of the royal family who filled a power vacuum' caused by the death of Neferefre. In this schema, Shepseskare succeeds Neferefre instead of Neferirkare, but in both Lloyd's (2010) and Morby and Rozier's (2014) chronologies, Shepseskare is placed immediately after Neferirkare. What is clear here is that we lack a detailed understanding of the Egyptian succession in the mid 25th century BCE.

There was also a rebellion at Thebes during Ptolemy VI's reign (Morkot 2010, 179). In 145 BCE, the king received a fatal wound in a battle in Syria (Clayton 1994, 212). Description: (Ptolemy VI and Ptolemy VIII needs more work. Transition was contested, whenever we consider this to be - reign start date needs to be looked at again, perhaps the order of kingship. The entire period is complicated by the long civil war with Ptolemy VI. If coded as multiple reigns, in one reign Ptolemy VIII was overthrown.). Ptolemy VIII came to the throne after murdering his nephew and stepson Ptolemy VII (Clayton 1994, 213-14). There was a long civil war between Ptolemy VI and his brother Ptolemy VIII, which 'frequently involved the actions of the [Alexandrian] mob' (Lloyd 2000, 411). Ptolemy VIII was forced to flee the Alexandrian mob to Cyprus but then successfully reinvaded Egypt and survived as king of Egypt until 116 BCE (Clayton 1994, 214). Harsiesis, a rebel king, also launched a separatist rebellion in Thebes (Morkot 2010, 180). Morkot (2010, 180) mentions 'military actions throughout the country' during the civil war between Ptolemy VIII and Cleopatra II, but does not specify whether these were led by soldiers or by different elites commanding troops. When Ptolemy VIII died, the throne passed to his daughter Cleopatra III ruling jointly with her eldest son, Ptolemy IX Soter II.

Description: With Roman assistance, the exiled Ptolemy XII invaded Egypt and ascended to the throne for a second time (Clayton 1994, 215). Conflict.name: War between Cleopatra VII and Ptolemy III; Assassination of Ptolemy XIV
Description: (Queen was overthrown - code suicide as assassination?). Cleopatra VII faced opposition from her own brother Ptolemy XIII, who plotted with palace courtiers to overthrow her (Clayton 1994, 216). After his death by drowning, she married her younger brother Ptolemy XIV. After he in turn died, her son by Caesar, Ptolemy XV, came to the throne as co-ruler. When the Roman emperor Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BCE, she committed suicide, ushering in the Roman period of Egyptian history (Clayton 1994, 217). Her suicide was precipitated by the Roman invasion.

Description: (Killed in battle against foreign enemy is not assassination. No evidence for a contested transition. Not external interference either unless the Hyksos were attempting to conquer the north. This battle may have been an attempt at an Egyptian conquest of the Delta region? Certainly cannot code external interference if the war the king is killed in is his own invasion). Unlike his Seventeenth-Dynasty predecessors, who had maintained an 'uneasy truce' with the Hyksos kings in the north (Clayton 1994, 95), Seqenenre fought campaigns attempting to expel the Fifteenth-Dynasty rulers (Clayton 1994, 97). Violent injuries to his skull indicate that he was likely killed in battle, presumably against Hyksos forces (Clayton 1994, 96). His successor Kamose may have been his son, but this is uncertain (Bourriau 2000, 199). The sources do not mention popular uprisings or elite conflicts within the area of Theban control.
